blocks.text: “Don't say yes,” replies Miss Smallweed, “because I know what you girls are like. Do it without saying it, and then I may begin to believe you.”

Charley swallows a great gulp of tea to show that she obeys. In doing this, she breaks up the 'Druidical ruins'. Then Miss Smallweed tells her not to eat so greedily. “In you girls,” she says, this is disgusting. Charley might have found it harder to agree with Miss Smallweed's opinions about girls in general. But just then there is a knock at the door.
“See who it is, and don't chew when you open it!” cries Judy.

The girl she has been watching goes to the door. Miss Smallweed uses this chance to push the rest of the bread and butter together into a mess. She also throws two or three dirty teacups into the basin of tea. The tea in the basin is low, like the sea at low tide. In this way she shows that she thinks the eating and drinking are finished.
“Now! Who is it, and what's wanted?” says Judy in her sharp, bad-tempered way.
It seems that it is a man called “Mr. George.” Nobody announces him and there is no polite formality. Mr. George simply walks in.
“Whew!” says Mr. George. “You are hot here. Always a fire, eh? Well! Perhaps you are right to get used to one.” Mr. George says this last remark to himself, as he nods to Grandfather Smallweed.
“Ho! It's you!” cries the old gentleman. “How de do? How de do?”
“So-so,” replies Mr. George, and he sits down on a chair. “I have had the honor of seeing your granddaughter before. My respects to you, miss.”
“This is my grandson,” says Grandfather Smallweed. “You ha'n't seen him before. He is in the law, and not much at home.”

“My respects to him, too! He is like his sister. He is very like his sister. He is devilish like his sister,” says Mr. George. He puts great stress on the last strong word, and it is not completely a compliment.
“And how does the world treat you, Mr. George?” Grandfather Smallweed asks, slowly rubbing his legs.
“Pretty much as usual. Like a football.”

He is a man of fifty, with dark, sun-browned skin. He has a strong, well-shaped body and a good-looking face. His dark hair is short and stiff, his eyes are bright, and his chest is broad. His hands are strong and muscular, and as sunburnt as his face. They have clearly known a fairly rough life. There is something strange about him. He sits forward on his chair, as if from long habit. It is as though he is leaving space for some uniform or military equipment, but he has put all that away completely. His step, too, is slow, even and heavy. It would go well with the heavy clashing and jingling of spurs. He is close-shaved now. But his mouth looks as if his upper lip has had a large moustache for years. Sometimes he lays the open palm of his broad brown hand over his lip, and this gives the same impression. All in all, one might guess that Mr. George was once a trooper, a soldier on horseback.

Mr. George is very different from the Smallweed family. No trooper was ever sent to live in a house so unlike him. It is like comparing a broadsword with an oyster-knife. His body is large and fully grown, but their bodies are small and stunted. His manner is big, and it fills any amount of space. Their ways are little, narrow and mean. His voice is loud and full, but their voices are sharp and thin. These things are opposite in the strongest and strangest way. He sits in the middle of the gloomy sitting room, leaning a little forward. His hands are on his thighs and his elbows stick out to the sides. He looks as if he might swallow up the whole family if he stayed there long. He might swallow the whole four-roomed house too, with its extra little back kitchen and everything.
“Do you rub your legs to rub life into 'em?” he asks of Grandfather Smallweed, after looking round the room.
“Why, it's partly a habit, Mr. George, and—yes—it partly helps the blood move round my body,” he replies.
